title: Common Reformed view: God's goodness forbids creating man without original righteousness, prone to evil
source_text: XXXIV. Utcunque tamen de eo sit, & quacunque tandem ratione dicatur Originalis justitia primo homini fuisse naturalis, communis videtur esse Reformatorum sententia, omnino bonitati & sapientiae divinae repugnare, ut Deus hominem condat absque justitia Originali, & talem qui Deum, ut par est, non agnoscat & amet, & ad malum sit pronus atque proclivis, & in quo sensus atque appetitus rationi repugnant, & sint legi divinae rebelles. Nec enim existimant ejusmodi erga Deum amoris privationem, & praecipitem ad malum & vitia inclinationem, ac rebellionem sensus & appetitus adversus mentem, & legem divinam in creatura rationali posse peccato & culpa carere. Adeoque absurdum & creatori injurium ducunt, si dicatur ejusmodi inferiorum animae facultatum rebellionem, & quae inde sequitur totius hominis ad malum pronitatem, & repugnantiam ad bonum aliquid esse consequens hominis compositionem ex anima rationali & corpore organico, quodque necessario, & secundum ipsam rerum naturam inde resultat, nisi Deus aliquid supra naturam addat, quod subjiciat rationem Deo, & partem inferiorem animae rationi subdat.
pass_a_gloss: However that may be, and in whatever way finally Original justice is said to have been natural to the first man, the common opinion of the Reformed seems to be that it wholly conflicts with divine goodness and wisdom that God should found man without Original justice, and such a one as does not acknowledge and love God, as is right, and is prone and inclined to evil, and in whom sense and appetite fight against reason, and are rebels to the divine law. For they do not think that such privation of love toward God, and headlong inclination to evil and vices, and rebellion of sense and appetite against the mind, and the divine law, can in a rational creature lack sin and fault. And so they hold it absurd and injurious to the creator, if it is said that such rebellion of the lower faculties of the soul, and the proneness of the whole man to evil which follows from it, and repugnance to good, is something consequent on man's composition from rational soul and organic body, and which necessarily, and according to the very nature of things, results thence, unless God adds something above nature, which subjects reason to God, and subordinates the lower part of the soul to reason.
pass_b_english: However that may be, and on whatever ground original righteousness is said to have been natural to the first man, the common Reformed view seems to be that it is wholly at odds with God's goodness and wisdom for him to make man without original righteousness: a man who does not know and love God as he should, who leans and inclines toward evil, and in whom sense and appetite resist reason and rebel against God's law.

They do not believe that in a rational creature such a lack of love for God, such a headlong bent to evil and vice, and such a rebellion of sense and appetite against the mind and God's law, can be free of sin and guilt.

So they think it absurd, and an insult to the Creator, to say that this rebellion of the soul's lower faculties, with the proneness of the whole man to evil and his resistance to good that follow from it, is a consequence of man's being made of a rational soul and an organic body, something that results from that make-up necessarily and by the very nature of things unless God adds something above nature to subject reason to God and the lower part of the soul to reason.

choices.why: Culpa is moral guilt, not mere defect; the English says 'guilt'.
